q: The front office concludes that a new warmup protocol reduces soft-tissue injuries when in truth the protocol has no effect. Which error has been made?
o: Type II error
Sampling bias
Type I error
Regression to the mean
keyed_text: Type I error

q: In output for a patient survey, the item "Staff explained my medications clearly" has a communality of .12. What does this mean?
o: The item correlates .12 with the total score
12 percent of respondents skipped the item
The item loads .12 on every factor
Only about 12 percent of the item's variance is shared with the extracted factors
keyed_text: Only about 12 percent of the item's variance is shared with the extracted factors

q: "All students enrolled at Big Tree State in fall 2026" is best described as:
o: A sample
A population, if that is the group you want to conclude about
A parameter
A variable
keyed_text: A population, if that is the group you want to conclude about

q: A state report gives 95% intervals for mean per-pupil spending: Region A $9,100 to $9,600 and Region B $10,200 to $10,800. The intervals do not overlap. What does that support?
o: Proof that Region B spends more money on classroom instruction specifically
Reasonable evidence that the two regional means genuinely differ
Proof that the samples were the same size
Evidence that Region A's data are inaccurate
keyed_text: Reasonable evidence that the two regional means genuinely differ

q: Everything else held constant, which change would make the calculated t value in an independent-samples test larger in absolute size?
o: A larger alpha level
A larger standard error of the difference
A smaller sample in each group
A larger difference between the two group means
keyed_text: A larger difference between the two group means

q: With 40,000 student records, a district finds a 0.4-point difference on a 100-point test, p < .001. What is the right reading?
o: The difference is both statistically and practically important
The result is statistically significant but likely trivial in practice
The p-value proves the difference is large
The huge sample makes the p-value unreliable
keyed_text: The result is statistically significant but likely trivial in practice

q: One case in a completion model has a very large residual, but dropping it barely changes the coefficients. How is it best described?
o: A high leverage point in the model
Influential but not an outlier
Evidence of serious multicollinearity
An outlier that is not influential
keyed_text: An outlier that is not influential

q: A student wants Cronbach's alpha in JASP for a 10-item leadership self-efficacy scale. Which menu is the right starting point?
o: Regression > Linear Regression
Factor > Reliability Analysis
T-Tests > One Sample T-Test
Descriptives > Descriptive Statistics
keyed_text: Factor > Reliability Analysis

q: Which statement correctly pairs H0 and H1 for a study of a telehealth follow-up call?
o: H0: telehealth follow-up is better; H1: usual care follow-up is better
H0: the p-value is less than .05; H1: the p-value is greater than .05
H0: the patient sample is representative; H1: the patient sample is biased
H0: no difference in follow-up completion; H1: a difference exists
keyed_text: H0: no difference in follow-up completion; H1: a difference exists

q: On a clinic staff survey, the item "My manager listens to my concerns" has a loading of .78 on Factor 1. What does that number tell the analyst?
o: 78 percent of staff agreed with the item
The item is strongly associated with whatever underlying construct Factor 1 represents
The item correlates .78 with the total survey score
The item explains 78 percent of the variance in the survey
keyed_text: The item is strongly associated with whatever underlying construct Factor 1 represents

q: A team runs three separate t-tests comparing three clinics, each at alpha = .05. What is the problem?
o: Degrees of freedom can no longer be computed for any of the three comparisons
The outcome variable becomes ordinal
Each individual test loses all statistical power
The chance of at least one false positive rises well above 5 percent
keyed_text: The chance of at least one false positive rises well above 5 percent

q: A Broncos linebacker's 40-yard dash time sits 1.5 standard deviations BELOW the mean for his position group. Faster times are lower numbers. What does his z-score of -1.5 tell you?
o: He is faster than most linebackers in the group
He is slower than most linebackers in the group
He is exactly average because the sign is negative
His time cannot be compared to the group
keyed_text: He is faster than most linebackers in the group

q: An analyst removes a cross-loading item from a 15-item survey and reruns the analysis. What should she do next?
o: Report the original solution, since removal does not change results
Report both solutions and let readers pick
Re-examine the new loadings, eigenvalues, and alphas, because dropping an item can change the structure
Assume the remaining items are now unidimensional
keyed_text: Re-examine the new loadings, eigenvalues, and alphas, because dropping an item can change the structure

q: A memo states that mentoring hours caused higher retention, based on a regression of routinely collected personnel data. What is the problem?
o: Prediction from observational data cannot establish cause.
The analyst should have reported a correlation coefficient.
Causal claims require a considerably larger R-squared value.
Regression coefficients require experimental data to compute.
keyed_text: Prediction from observational data cannot establish cause.

q: A district scatterplot of class size against teacher-rated engagement shows a clear inverted-U shape, yet Pearson r is 0.03. What is the best conclusion?
o: The two variables are unrelated
There is a relationship, but it is curvilinear, so Pearson r near zero is misleading
The scatterplot must have been drawn incorrectly, since r and the plot always agree exactly
Sample size is too small for any correlation
keyed_text: There is a relationship, but it is curvilinear, so Pearson r near zero is misleading

q: An analyst computes both a 95% and a 99% confidence interval for the same mean using the same sample. How will the two intervals compare?
o: They will be identical in width
The 99% interval will be wider
The 99% interval will be narrower
The 99% interval will be shifted higher
keyed_text: The 99% interval will be wider

q: A nonprofit's 18-item volunteer survey yields four factors under the Kaiser criterion, but the scree plot clearly elbows after two, and the third and fourth factors have only two weak items each. What is a defensible decision?
o: Always take the Kaiser count, so retain four factors
Retain two factors, weighing the scree plot and interpretability alongside the eigenvalue rule
Retain all factors with any eigenvalue above zero
Rerun the analysis with only the items that loaded on factors 3 and 4
keyed_text: Retain two factors, weighing the scree plot and interpretability alongside the eigenvalue rule

q: A polling firm reports a candidate at 52 percent with a margin of error of 3 points. What does the margin reflect?
o: The interviewers' error rate
The bias introduced by question wording
The share of voters who refused to answer
Expected sampling variation around the estimate
keyed_text: Expected sampling variation around the estimate

q: In JASP, a student wants means, standard deviations, and a histogram for a set of continuous items. Where does she start?
o: Descriptives > Descriptive Statistics
Regression > Correlation Matrix
Frequencies > Binomial Test
ANOVA > Repeated Measures ANOVA
keyed_text: Descriptives > Descriptive Statistics

q: Both kinds of statistics are useful. The common mistake is:
o: Using descriptive statistics at all
Reporting a descriptive summary of a self-selected group as if it described everyone
Using inferential statistics on large samples
Reporting a mean
keyed_text: Reporting a descriptive summary of a self-selected group as if it described everyone

q: Students in a persistence model are clustered in 20 advising cohorts, and outcomes within a cohort move together. Which assumption is most at risk?
o: Homoscedasticity of residuals
Normality of the residuals
Linearity of relationships
Independence of errors
keyed_text: Independence of errors

q: A report concludes, 'We accept the null hypothesis: the two training formats are identical.' How should this be rewritten?
o: We failed to reject the null and found no evidence of a difference
We reject the alternative hypothesis with something close to 95 percent certainty
We have proved that the two training formats produce the very same outcomes
We accept the null hypothesis because the p-value turned out to exceed alpha
keyed_text: We failed to reject the null and found no evidence of a difference

q: A county compares two clinics and finds a difference much larger than typical sampling variation would produce. What does that support?
o: That measurement error in the two clinics' records is unusually high
That the numbers of patients sampled at the two clinics were equal
That the difference is unlikely under the null
That the difference between the clinics is large enough to matter in practice
keyed_text: That the difference is unlikely under the null

q: A nonprofit's evaluator writes, "There is a 95% probability that the true mean donation lies between $88 and $104." A statistician objects. What is the technical problem with that sentence?
o: The dollar range is too narrow for a donation study
Probability statements require a 99% confidence level
The true mean is fixed; the 95% describes the procedure, not this interval
Donations are usually skewed, so no confidence interval can legitimately be built here
keyed_text: The true mean is fixed; the 95% describes the procedure, not this interval

q: An academy fitness coach reports that a trialist's sprint time has a z-score of -2.0 on a normally distributed scouting measure where lower times are faster. What does this indicate?
o: The time is two standard deviations slower than average
The time is two standard deviations faster than average
The time sits near the 50th percentile
The z-score cannot be read without the raw mean
keyed_text: The time is two standard deviations faster than average

q: An exploratory factor analysis of a patient instrument produces a factor defined by exactly one item. What is the usual concern?
o: A factor defined by one item is not a construct summary; it usually signals the item is unrelated to the rest
Single-item factors inflate the eigenvalues of the other factors
Single-item factors should be retained because they are the purest
The analysis should be rerun with orthogonal rotation to merge it
keyed_text: A factor defined by one item is not a construct summary; it usually signals the item is unrelated to the rest

q: A grant report states that a correlation of r = 0.28 was significant at p < .05 with n = 400. Which statement best reflects both significance and magnitude?
o: The relationship is strong because p is small
Significance and magnitude are the same property
Because p < .05, about 5 percent of the variance is unexplained
The relationship is unlikely to be chance, but it explains only about 8 percent of the variance
keyed_text: The relationship is unlikely to be chance, but it explains only about 8 percent of the variance

q: A pilot finds that copilot users complete a task 6 minutes faster on average, with a pooled standard deviation of 12 minutes. What is Cohen's d, and how is it conventionally described?
o: d = 0.50, a medium effect
d = 2.00, a very large effect
d = 0.06, a negligible effect
d = 6.00, a large effect
keyed_text: d = 0.50, a medium effect

q: You survey 200 of 4,000 students and use the result to say something about all 4,000. That is:
o: Descriptive
Inferential — you are reasoning beyond the people you actually measured
A census
Invalid by definition
keyed_text: Inferential — you are reasoning beyond the people you actually measured

q: In a model predicting donor gift amount from years of giving and events attended, the intercept is 45. What does that represent?
o: The average gift amount across all of the donors
The smallest gift amount observed in the sample
The predicted gift when both predictors equal zero
The share of gift variance left unexplained
keyed_text: The predicted gift when both predictors equal zero

q: Two predictors in a staff retention model correlate .93, and both carry high VIF values. What is a reasonable response?
o: Drop one of them or combine them into a composite.
Raise alpha to .10 so that both stay significant.
Transform the outcome variable and rerun the model.
Report both coefficients without further comment.
keyed_text: Drop one of them or combine them into a composite.

q: A researcher repeatedly draws samples of 50 from a district and plots the sample means. What is being built?
o: The distribution of scores for every student in the whole district population
A distribution of the individual student scores collected across the samples
A sampling distribution of the mean
A distribution of p-values generated under the alternative hypothesis
keyed_text: A sampling distribution of the mean

q: A nonprofit reports p = .03 for a difference in job-placement rates between two program sites. What does that p-value actually mean?
o: There is only a 3 percent chance that the null hypothesis of no difference is true
There is a 97 percent chance the program itself caused the site-to-site difference
A difference this large would be rare if the null were true
The difference is large enough to change how the nonprofit should run the program
keyed_text: A difference this large would be rare if the null were true

q: A wellness pilot shows no significant difference but a moderate effect size with 25 participants. What is the sensible next step?
o: Conclude that the wellness program does not work for these participants
Report only the p-value, since that is the formal test of the hypothesis
Switch to a one-tailed test on the same data to see whether p drops below .05
Replicate with a larger sample, since power was low
keyed_text: Replicate with a larger sample, since power was low

q: Residuals plotted against predicted values form a clear U shape in a model of time to degree. What should the analyst conclude?
o: The relationship is not linear as modeled.
The sample is too small for this model.
One case is exerting excessive influence.
The errors are correlated across the cases.
keyed_text: The relationship is not linear as modeled.

q: A model of time to degree yields b = -0.35 for hours of advising received. How is that sign read?
o: Advising hours were reverse coded by the software.
The model fits the observed data rather poorly.
More advising predicts a shorter time to degree.
Advising hours and time to degree are unrelated here.

q: On a scatterplot, points fall almost exactly along a line running from the upper left to the lower right. What is the approximate correlation?
o: Close to zero
Close to +1.00
Close to -1.00
Cannot be estimated from a plot

q: An institutional researcher compares average engagement scores across three campuses in SPSS. Which path is correct?

Analyze > Compare Means > Paired-Samples T Test

q: Output for a 15-item survey lists the "total variance explained" table with initial eigenvalues and then rotated sums of squared loadings. What typically changes after rotation?

The eigenvalues become negative
The variance is redistributed more evenly across the retained factors, while the total they explain stays the same

q: A superintendent reports r = 0.40 between attendance rate and end-of-year math scores. What percent of the variance in math scores is shared with attendance?
o: 40 percent
16 percent
20 percent
64 percent

q: A survey of parents doubles its sample from 400 to 1,600. What happens to the standard error of the mean?
o: It doubles
It stays the same because the population is unchanged
It becomes zero
It gets smaller, so estimates are more precise

The intercept should be reported as a percentage

q: Regression output includes an ANOVA table with a Regression row and a Residual row. What does the F ratio there compare?
o: Each predictor measured against all the other predictors
Observed frequencies measured against expected ones
Variance explained by the model against variance unexplained
Adjusted R-squared measured against the raw R-squared

q: How does adjusted R-squared differ from R-squared in a multiple regression of program completion?

It penalizes the model for predictors relative to sample size.
It is always the larger of the two values reported.
It reports statistical significance rather than variance.

o: Roughly 64% to 72%
Roughly 66% to 70%
Roughly 60% to 76%
Exactly 68%, since that is the measured value

q: The front office wants a narrower confidence interval for mean concessions spending per fan without lowering the confidence level. Which change accomplishes this?

Report the standard deviation instead of the standard error
Raise the confidence level to 99 percent
Survey only fans seated in the Cauldron

Whether the gain justifies the cost

q: A random sample of 36 case managers reports a mean caseload of 40 clients with a standard deviation of 12. Using the 95% rule, which interval is correct?

An internal AI-readiness score is scaled to a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15 in a normal distribution. A manager says any unit scoring above 130 is elite. Roughly what share of units clears that bar?
o: About 16 percent
About 2 percent
About 30 percent
About 50 percent

q: Factor analysis of a climate survey yields a four-item "Trust in Leadership" subscale with alpha = .88. What does the pair of results together support?

That the subscale is valid for all populations
That the subscale has more explanatory power than the other subscales

q: A research office is deciding how to store a cleaned survey dataset for future staff. Which combination is best practice?

The .sav file with labeled variables plus the syntax used to clean and analyze it
A screenshot library of each analysis window
The original paper surveys plus a summary memo

q: A leadership team wants the Pearson correlation between staff tenure and patient-satisfaction scores in SPSS. Which path do they use?
o: Analyze > Regression > Curve Estimation
Analyze > Descriptive Statistics > Ratio
Analyze > Compare Means > Means
Analyze > Correlate > Bivariate

q: Increasing within-group variability while holding group means constant will generally do what to the F ratio?
o: Increase it
Decrease it
Leave it unchanged
Make it negative

q: An analyst has 14 items and wants to know whether reducing them is even worth attempting. Which pair of checks speaks most directly to that question?

The scree plot and the response rate

q: A hospital is deciding whether to change a medication protocol, where an error would be costly. Compared with a 95% interval, what does choosing a 99% interval accomplish?
o: It guarantees the decision will be correct
It shrinks the range of plausible values

It increases the sample size automatically
